The Moonstone. Wilkie Collins's 1868 novel is considered the first detective novel in English literature. It centers on the theft of a valuable Indian diamond from an English country house during a celebration. The narrative unfolds through multiple perspectives as detective Sergeant Cuff investigates the case, uncovering a web of family secrets and complex motivations.

A large diamond called the Moonstone, stolen from an Indian temple, is given as a gift to Rachel Verinder on her eighteenth birthday. The diamond vanishes on the same night, and suspicion falls on Indian jugglers who have been loitering around the house. Sergeant Cuff, the famous detective from Scotland Yard, is called in to investigate. He quickly identifies an unlikely suspect.

The novel unfolds through different narrators—servants, family members, and the detective—each revealing new pieces of the puzzle. Rachel Verinder herself is revealed to be the thief, taken in her sleep under the influence of opium administered for medical reasons. The real plot involves a complicated love story and family loyalty. Rachel took the diamond to protect her family honor from suspicion. Indian Brahmins are ultimately connected to the stone's fate, and the resolution involves themes of cultural appropriation and restitution.

Sergeant Cuff pioneered the professional detective archetype and appears in other Collins works. The Moonstone laid the foundation for all English detective fiction that followed, standing as a foundational example of the sensational novel that blends mystery with social commentary.
